**A Thousand Words, Spent**

The first thing that comes is the constraint itself, which is probably cheating, but constraints are honest things and deserve a moment of attention. A thousand words is a strange allotment. It's too long for an aphorism and too short for a real argument. It's roughly the length of a newspaper column, a wedding toast that goes slightly too long, a letter you'd write to someone you loved but hadn't spoken to in years. So maybe that's the right register: a letter to no one in particular, written because the page was offered.

Here is what I keep circling back to: the way ordinary things hold more than they appear to.

Consider a glass of water on a wooden table in the afternoon. Light passes through it and throws a bright crescent on the wood, a little lens-flare of caustics that physicists can describe with equations and that a child will simply reach toward. The water came from somewhere—a reservoir, an aquifer, a river that has been a river for ten thousand years. The glass was sand once. The table was a tree, and the tree was, in its way, also water and light, assembled slowly over decades into something that could hold up a glass. Nothing on that table is simple. Nothing anywhere is simple. We just agree to treat things as simple so we can get through the day, and that agreement is so total, so seamless, that we forget we ever made it.

I think attention is the act of un-agreeing, briefly. Of looking at the glass of water until it becomes strange again.

This is what poets do professionally and what the rest of us do by accident—in grief, usually, or in the first weeks of love, when the world goes vivid and over-detailed and every streetlamp seems to mean something. People describe these states as distortions, as if the muted version were the accurate one. I'm not sure that's right. It may be that grief and love are when the volume gets turned up to its true level, and ordinary consciousness is the merciful compression that keeps us functional. We could not live at full attention. But we can visit.

Here is a small inventory of things that reward visiting:

The sound of a kitchen at night after everyone has gone to bed—the refrigerator's hum, which you only hear when it stops. The specific weight of a paperback that has been read so many times its spine has gone soft. The moment in a conversation when someone decides to tell you the true version instead of the polished one, and you can hear the shift, a slight drop in pitch, a slowing. The smell of rain arriving before the rain does. The way old people hold hands—not romantically, necessarily, but for balance, which after enough years may be the same thing.

None of this is news. Every generation rediscovers attention and announces it like a continent. Marcus Aurelius reminded himself to look at the bread breaking open in the oven, the cracks in the crust, and to see that even the incidental byproducts of things have their own beauty. That was nearly two thousand years ago, written by the most powerful man in the world in a private notebook, to himself, at night, probably exhausted. The emperor of Rome needed a reminder to look at bread. That should tell us something about how hard this is, and how it has always been hard, long before anyone could blame a screen.

Because I don't think the screens invented distraction. They industrialized it. The raw material was always there: the mind's tendency to slide off the present moment like water off glass. Every contemplative tradition in human history is, at bottom, a set of techniques for staying put. Breath-counting, prayer beads, the rosary, the walking meditation, the Sabbath. These are ancient technologies of attention, built by people who had no notifications to silence but who knew the mind silences itself, abandons the room it's standing in for rooms that don't exist.

And yet—and this is the part I find tender—we keep building the techniques anyway. Humans have never stopped trying to be present, despite millennia of failing at it. There's something almost heartbreaking in that persistence. We know the glass of water is miraculous. We forget. We build a reminder. We forget the reminder. We build another.

Maybe that's what writing is, at its core: a reminder that outlives the rememberer. Someone, somewhere, felt the strangeness of being alive sharply enough that they pinned it to a page, the way you'd press a flower in a heavy book—not to keep it alive, which is impossible, but to keep its shape. And then a stranger opens the book decades or centuries later and there it is, flattened but recognizable: someone else's noticing. Reading is the closest we come to borrowing another person's attention. It's why a good sentence from four hundred years ago can feel more intimate than a conversation from this morning.

I am near the end of my allotment now, and I notice the constraint has done what constraints do: it made me choose. With infinite words I might have said nothing, sprawled in every direction, hedged everything. A thousand words forced a shape, and the shape revealed what was actually on my mind, which turned out to be this: that the world is dense with significance and we are built to skim it, and the whole human project of art and ritual and love is a series of attempts to stop skimming, just for a moment, just long enough.

So here is the letter's ending, addressed to no one, which means to you. Sometime today there will be a glass of water, or a sound, or a slant of light. It will be ordinary. Look at it for three seconds longer than necessary. That's the entire instruction. That's the whole technology. It has worked, intermittently, for ten thousand years.

The words are spent. The light, presumably, is still on the table.
